slides.title: Ray Tracing With Conformal Geometry
slides.notes: Open by making the lecture an engineering stress test for conformal geometry. The point is not that every value must be stored as a full conformal blade. The point is that points, rays, rounds, flats, normals, and spawned rays can be named in one language, then specialized where repeated rendering queries demand cheaper storage.

slides.title: Pipeline: Narrow The Question
slides.notes: Use the pipeline as the organizing map for the whole class. Each stage narrows the geometric question from a pixel-sized viewing query to a local surface event. Emphasize that every later stage depends on preserving the answer of the earlier predicates, so speedups must be justified by invariants rather than by hope.

slides.title: Rays Bridge Conformal Lines And Hot Loops
slides.notes: Frame this slide as the translation layer. In conformal language a Euclidean point lifts to a null point and a line can be built algebraically. In the inner loop, however, the renderer stores an origin, a unit direction, and a parameter interval because closest-hit comparisons and spawned ray offsets read those fields constantly.

slides.title: Spheres And Planes Are Early Predicates
slides.notes: Make conservative rejection concrete. A bounding sphere hit does not prove the mesh is hit; it only permits more expensive work. A sphere miss, or a plane interval outside the ray segment, is a certificate that later triangle tests are unnecessary. This is where conformal rounds and flats become acceleration-minded predicates.

slides.title: Triangle Hits Carry Barycentric Data
slides.notes: Slow down on barycentric weights because they are the bridge between intersection and shading. The ray parameter tells where the surface lies along the viewing query, while the three weights say whether the hit is inside the triangle and how normals, colors, or texture coordinates should be interpolated.

slides.title: Normals Turn Hits Into Surface Attitude
slides.notes: Treat normals as local surface attitude, not as decorative arrows. The mesh is intersected as flat triangles, but the shader may use an interpolated unit normal to represent smoother lighting. That compromise is mathematically honest only when the notebook checks positive areas, unit normals, and transformed model invariants.

slides.title: Reflection And Refraction Spawn New Rays
slides.notes: Connect the vector formulas to the algebraic habit students already know. Reflection is a sandwich-style operation in geometric algebra and a short dot-product formula in the shader. Refraction adds Snell's law and the possibility of total internal reflection, so the ray-spawning rule must return either a unit direction or a principled failure.

slides.title: Acceleration Keeps The Answer But Changes The Work
slides.notes: Separate correctness from cost. The BSP traversal is allowed to change the order and number of primitive tests, but it is not allowed to change the closest hit or miss result. The notebook's ray bundle comparison is the right evidence: agreement of answers first, then fewer triangle tests as the payoff.

slides.title: Shading Is Local Geometry Plus Visibility
slides.notes: At the shading stage, the ray tracer stops asking which surface is first and starts asking which outgoing directions matter. The hit point, normal, view direction, finite shadow segment, light direction, and reflected ray are all local geometric objects. Color is the result of those objects passing visibility and angle tests.

slides.title: The Design Habit: Algebra Names, Code Specializes
slides.notes: Close by turning the chapter into a reusable software habit. Let conformal geometry name the object and the invariant, let the implementation store the cheapest representation that answers the repeated query, and keep executable checks between the two. That bridge is the practical lesson students can carry into any geometry-heavy renderer.
